articles.title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
articles.content: Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets. The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia. Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware. Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions. On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices. The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with. "Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said. The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice. “[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger . Yesterday, Ledger provided another update , confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.” While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware. Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires. The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong. According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM. "Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained . Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)." articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
articles.content: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard. As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. articles.title: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
articles.content: An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody. An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco. Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said. OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted. Surveillance footage shows Alfozan near the room on multiple dates before the discovery, though he was not authorized to enter the room or attend meetings there, prosecutors said. Meetings in the room frequently involved confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and government engagements, according to the complaint. Prosecutors say this image shows Alfozan looking behind a television in an OpenAI conference room.​ | Source: Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California Before the device was installed, Alfozan used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities, and calendars, as well as the locations of leadership and outside partner meetings, the complaint alleges. A chatbot account tied to Alfozan’s spouse, which shared identifiers with his own account, submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 about building, installing, obscuring, and remotely accessing a recording device, prosecutors said. Queries included how to “build a continuous audio recorder” and “encrypt the SD card,” prosecutors claimed. On Sept. 27 and 28, the account asked about the specific device that was later found, including its unique MAC address. articles.title: Show HN: Guitoro, a virtual guitar you strum with your keyboard
articles.content: The most complete virtual guitar online: four instruments, every key, real chord shapes, songs, a backing band and recording, all free in one place. Four real instruments Steel-string acoustic, classic guitar, electric and four-string bass, each built from recorded samples. Pick a recording for the acoustic (Warm, Bright or Mellow) and the classic (Natural or Concert), and presets for the electric, from Clean to Crunch, Classic Rock, Metal, Lead and Ambient. 15 chords in every key Pick any of the 24 major and minor keys and the chord keys fill with the chords that fit it: the main chords, sevenths, and sus, add9 or sus2 colors. Edit puts any chord you type, like F#m7 or Dsus2, on a key. Chord shapes on the neck While a chord rings, the neck shows finger numbers, barres, muted strings and the capo. Standard is the shape most players learn first, Easy swaps a barre chord for a smaller shape, and Up plays the same chord higher up the neck. Songs at any speed 51 songs and classical pieces come set up to play, from Wonderwall and Hotel California to Canon in D. Slow them to 20%, lead their chords from the keys, or play along on your own guitar. 56 strum and picking patterns 14 everyday strums from Steady downs and the pop staple D DU U DU to shuffle and 6/8, 4 styles (reggae, funk and country), 26 more rhythms drawn from real songs, and 12 picking patterns like Travis and classical p-i-m-a. Choose one and you hear it straight away. A backing band Drums, bass and strings that follow your chords: 15 drum styles, including rock, funk, reggae, bossa nova and cajon, and 25 bass lines. The Band switch next to Play turns them on. Tempo goes from 10 to 220 BPM, with a metronome. Your own songs Paste a song from a chord site or as ChordPro text, pick a strum, and Guitoro plays it with the band. Write "x2" to repeat a line or a part. Lyrics are left out, and your songs stay in your browser. Solo mode Play single notes and melodies on the neck from the computer keyboard, with hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato. Amp & FX Overdrive, distortion and fuzz on the electric, plus bass, mid and treble, room or hall reverb, and delay on every instrument. Tunings and capo 10 tunings, from Standard, Drop D and half step down to DADGAD and Open G, D and E, a capo up to fret 10, and a left-handed guitar. Record and export Record takes of up to 10 minutes with the band, replay them and save them as WAV or a small compressed file. Takes stay in your browser. Online tuner A free guitar tuner that listens through your microphone, with pages for drop D, open tunings, the bass and the ukulele .

articles.title: I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI bot traffic
articles.content: For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io , a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed. A month ago, I posted it to HN , and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then… My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load. So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!). Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked. Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc. The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users. articles.title: A plea not to use uv-build
articles.content: After seeing yet another dozen packages lose keywords on Gentoo because of a single key dependency switching to uv-build , I would like to plea on behalf of Gentoo users: please don’t use uv-build as a build backend. Just to be clear, this is not about uv itself or any other Astral tools; these are good tools with a nice and responsive upstream. The uv-build backend is one thing we have to disagree on. I’m not saying it’s bad; I’m saying that its benefits don’t outweigh the drawbacks. What are the drawbacks? It’s really big and it’s written in Rust. Rust has many advantages, but none of them really matter for a build backend that is used to build pure Python packages. It’s a huge dependency (as of 0.13.0, its wheels are between 1.2 MiB and 1.5 MiB, depending on the platform) and it has no benefit over using a small pure Python backend (say, flit-core whose wheel is 45 KiB). It means that all Gentoo users need to build it from source, and given that it’s released quite frequently (12 releases in the 30 days prior to writing this post), that’s a lot of building. Like, for every 100 ms spent running uv-build to install one release of your package, Gentoo users will spend many hours building new uv-build versions over and over again. However, build times aren’t the biggest problem; portability is. You can run Python pretty much anywhere where you can get a working C compiler. Some minor features may not work, but the core is reasonably portable. The list of platforms supported by Rust is growing slowly, and even if you can get a working Rust compiler on a given platform, uv may not work. The problems can range from bugs in the lot of packages that uv depends on (for example, rustix::fs and its dependencies skipping SPARC, for no apparent reason ), to the resulting executable being so big that the toolchain runs out of address space (and unlike system memory, you can’t really add address space to a system; the Gentoo uv ebuild already carries two hacks to make it possible to build uv on 32-bit platforms). And then, if your platform is not supported at all… well, let’s just say that adding and maintaining a new platform is a full-time job that may involve a lot of swearing at the code churn. What about the advantages? Well, I’m aware of two reasons to use uv-build. One is consistency with using uv for your project, and it doesn’t really matter. It’s a backend and the whole point of PEP 517 is that you can use any backend with any tool. You can use flit-core, you can use hatchling , and either of them will work just fine with uv (or any other frontend). The other reason is performance and that argument makes even less sense. Even if it mattered, we’re realistically talking about a difference in the ballpark of 100 ms, for an action executed rarely; it is equally possible that any gain will be outweighed by the time needed to fetch the 1.5 MiB wheel for uv-build. But it doesn’t matter, because realistically the backend is only used by project developers,

articles.title: Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution?
articles.content: Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution? October 12, 2026 The last blog post I wrote explained why I chose to make FairScan open source . In particular, I said I knew there was a risk when I published FairScan's code and I was ready to accept it. I didn't expect to face that reality so soon. What happened to me over the past few weeks I had never heard of Ente before September 16. On that day, I received an email from one of their engineers. The message thanked me for FairScan and announced that the Ente Locker app now used FairScan's segmentation model as part of a new document scanning feature. It referred to a blog post that credited FairScan's model and claimed that Ente "wrote the image processing around it from scratch" . articles.title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd??
articles.content: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?? October 12, 2026 Hacker News Lobsters vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd , but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as: VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control […] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3). Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster. Or so it would , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue: VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS ? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)! I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd / ps / sd / ss or 132 / 213 / 231 , which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version. I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that. If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer. Update seastarer and 039234562456 gave me enough pointers to crack this. Back in 2023, Intel failed to add AVX-512 support to consumer CPUs due to hardware limitations, but still wanted to add some goodies from AVX-512. That’s how AVX10 was born – a new extension that looked roughly like AVX-512, but had conditional support for 512-bit vector lengths. AVX-512 uses a strange ins

articles.title: The reverts will continue until morale improves
articles.content: Many readers will be aware that an unusually high number of features have been reverted from the PostgreSQL 19 branch after the beta period began. Having some reverts is not unusual, maybe one per cycle could be expected. But this time around, about 8 to 10 significant features, depending on how you count, have been reverted, and some of them quite late in the beta period. I have been on the receiving end of some of that, as the developer or committer of some of those features, and have gotten some questions about it, and so I want to take a moment to reflect on this. I’ll try to extrapolate a little bit to similarly affected work that I was not actively involved in, but these are just my opinions at this point. So what happened? I don’t think we, meaning all the developers affected, have had enough time to fully reflect on all this. But here are some thoughts. It’s probably a combination of these, and a different combination in the case of each reverted feature. Maybe we just didn’t do a good enough job. Maybe the code was just not good enough. We’ll learn and improve. It’s probably some of that, and I’m mentioning it here to not give the impression that it was only the other factors that I’m going to mention. It could also be a coincidence. Maybe we had been on such a good roll that we attempted to tackle several features that turned out to be too hard, or at least too hard to finish in time. Some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta. But there was also a long tail of relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases. In past times, many of these would not have surfaced until much later and we would have fixed them bit by bit over the subsequent five years. But with LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time. Most if not all of the affected reverted features were written a long time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles. A corollary of that is that, at least for the most part, as far as I can tell, this situation is not due to “vibe coding”. This code was written well before that was a possibility. Because of the Vulnpocalypse, many senior developers were busy between, say, April (the start of feature freeze for PostgreSQL 19, and also the start of the Vulnpocalypse) and August (the most recent PostgreSQL security release) with working on fixes for security issues. articles.title: Where is all the new, good software?
articles.content: Where is all the new, good software? 12 Oct, 2026 Here's a question we see, especially from AI skeptics: if AI coding is so great, shouldn't we be seeing more new, good software by now? Here are some answers. As usual in this style of post, these are conjectural, candidate answers, and I would give some of them little weight. We are in fact seeing software improvement, in the form of fewer bugs and better performance. We are in fact seeing software improvement, in the form of more and better features in existing products. We are in fact seeing software improvement, but the "we" is very limited. Most people don't adopt new software very often, so it's not surprising that they aren't finding new great software now. Many businesses' software-development processes have subsystems, especially political subsystems, that have not been accelerated with AI. (Imagine the process of getting senior engineers and product managers to sign off on a development plan. The engineers and PMs could use AI to do this better and faster, but perhaps they aren't yet doing that.) AI is replacing more durable, longer-lasting software with more ephemeral forms of software or software use, and one might not easily perceive this as "better software via AI." (If you do your taxes with Claude and don't bother building or shopping for better tax-preparation software, you don't quite get the "this product is like TurboTax but wonderful" experience, however much you might benefit.) AI is replacing broadly available software with private software. Domain experts are building their own tools; executives are making their own dashboards; companies have bespoke internal projects. So the software is out there, just not visible to the rest of us, and especially not visible to skeptics. We're making more software instead of making software better . We've always had the choice of (roughly) improving what exists or pushing development forward, and we've often chosen the latter. It's not surprising that we're still doing a lot of the latter. Software teams are capturing a lot of the speedup in the form of more leisure or quasi-leisure time. (To greatly simplify: software teams are offering 2x speedups to their companies. They're then using tools that allow them to work 10x as efficiently, and taking nice long coffee breaks.) AI improvements in software sometimes push us to use and make software less . Sometimes AI helps me figure out that a software project is a bad idea. Sometimes it nudges me to spend more analog time with humans. Sometimes it helps me find, and encourages me to read, more and better books. The net effect of this for me still involves my spending way more time making and using software, but it might be different for others. Most of the time, we're improving not just software but some system with both software and non-software components. articles.content: Back in August I mentioned the new curl performance tests we have running. I figured it could be apt to return to this topic just to mention some of the initial outcomes. When the team gets a new set of charts, graphs and plots that visualize something, like performance, they offer an excellent opportunity for us to try to make them look better. This new setup is no exception. The performance tests have only been running for just a little over two months but they have already made us improve curl performance in several areas. Of course, for most transfers these changes won’t make many visible differences to users. This is more in the vein that every little bit counts and that nothing should run slower than it has to. This is a list of some improvements that are included in the curl 8.23.0 release, to be shipped tomorrow on October 14. faster base64 encoding and decoding With a few different changes, the internal base64 encoding function is more than twice as fast, while base64 decoding is 40% faster. faster URL encoding and decoding Meaning percent encoding the octets that are not safe to use in URLs. The decoding function now runs more than twice as fast compare to before, while the encoding function is around four times as fast. faster date parsing Converting a date provided in plain ASCII text, as is used in for example cookie headers, to the epoch – number of seconds since Jan 1st 1970, is now more than twice as fast as before. Mostly thanks to completely replaced functions for week day, month name and time zone name lookups. faster URL parsing Parsing a full URL to split it up into separate components as well as confirming its validity is a core component of curl, and libcurl exposes this functionality in its API. articles.title: Living in the Weimar era of Ruby
articles.content: Much has been said about the DHH keynote that he gave at RailsWorld. To me, it was the voice of a person in an existential crisis, but also a very jaded one. “Look how I don’t care anymore, and you should not care either” is not a great message when you are the headline speaker at the conference - let’s call it CareConf - that you have, yourself, lobbied for. The message from the supreme leader was clear: we vibe-rewrote HEY in a more performant way, it worked great, we neither need nor care about Rails anymore. I honestly believe that, instead of amassing even more applause via vitriolic truth-bombing, he could have just left the toy he no longer loves - including its community - in peace. But here is the thing: the rich and famous losing interest in the good stuff does not oblige the rest of us to. If anything, it frees up the room. 🧭 I am currently available for contract work. Hire me to help make your Rails app better! I must admit that for a few days I felt very depressed about it all. Not about “AIs writing all the code” - that much is clear to me, and I do not lament the changing landscape of the craft - I do lament the landscape of usage , which is a topic for another article. It is abundantly clear that the LLMs are here to stay, that typing every single line by hand is no longer sustainable, and that the scales have shifted profoundly. What made me depressed was just how little care there was about the Ruby ecosystem and community, and the disdain with which David flushed the entire Rails and Ruby culture down the drain for the sake of “running it on a single Raspberry Pi”, as he put it. What I am actually observing is something different: a renaissance, even though quite a few prominent Rubyists have moved on to other stacks - which are now much more open to exploration, as you don’t have to write all that… gunk - let’s call it what it is - by hand. A detailed unpack of 7 little-endian integers is not particularly interesting, nor artistic - it’s just gunk, and I won’t miss it. Unless struct packing is needed to make it fast, but then we can always art-direct additionally. There was an interesting time in German history, right between the two World Wars - the “interbellum”, the time of the Weimar Republic. It was very turbulent, and a lot of it wasn’t pretty in the slightest - social difficulties, unemployment, incredible inflation, squalid living conditions, the emergence of the wildest movements, cabarets and cults imaginable… but there was also something else. The “Roaring Twenties” of Weimar Germany also produced an incredible number of great, whimsical, fascinating artistic movements. From the Bauhaus to the Berlin gay cabarets, from Kurt Weill to Fritz Lang’s Metropolis - it was a booming time, and a lot of what appeared then is still valued and cherished today. And it was a technological boom as well - the ever more widespread use of electricity, the large-scale deployment of modern pharmaceuticals, the subways, the automobile…

articles.title: Lotus Improv on the NeXT
articles.content: It is spoken of in reverent tones, invoked like a magic spell, whispered about as one of the mythical "roads not taken" in computing history. Its proponents write glowing reports and fawning YouTube reviews, lamenting its failure in the historical marketplace, each offering some justification for it not having set the world ablaze. It is safe to say, the legend of Lotus Improv persists to this day. If we put ourselves in Steve Jobs's shoes circa 1988, it's easy to see why he would have been smitten by an early preview of what we now call a "pivot table." NeXT was struggling to find its market, and exclusives which justified a system purchase were sorely needed. "Maybe Improv can do for NeXT what VisiCalc did for the Apple II," must surely have crossed Jobs's mind. In making it a NeXT exclusive, Improv seemed to be a clear-eyed, forward-looking answer to the question dogging the company, posed by the inaugural issue of NeXTWORLD Magazine , "Why NeXT?" NeXTWORLD Magazine , Editor-in-Chief Michael Miley, for his first column "Black Box". The TL;DR of the answer was that NeXT is a "new type of computer," an "interpersonal computer," the first to be built from the ground up for "collaborative computing." Both NeXT and Improv brought innovative solutions to their respective computing questions of the day. NeXT made UNIX palatable to those scared of the terminal, debuted Display Postscript on a mega-pixel display, and made development for the system a snap. Improv rethought multi-dimensional data modeling, offered English-like formulas, and made it easy to rearrange data views on a whim. The bones of both remain to this day. NeXT's operating system, NeXTSTEP / OPENSTEP, morphed into macOS, and by extension iOS. Lotus abandoned Improv fairly quickly, but a quick survey of today's spreadsheets shows a universal embrace of pivot tables. Even today, it feels like nothing else, and still does data tricks no other spreadsheet can do as elegantly. Given its mythos, I feel a kind of nerd obligation to love it. And yet... articles.title: Creusot 0.14.0 release - Contracts for Rust, formally proved
articles.content: We are pleased to announce the release of version 0.14.0 of Creusot , our formal verification tool for Rust. In this post, we highlight a small selection of new features. See the full changelog for the rest. What's new in Creusot? Partial orders Previously, Creusot restricted its specification of PartialOrd to total orders. Since version 0.13.0, we have relaxed it to allow partial orders. (We skipped a devlog entry for 0.13.0 so let's talk about this here.) Our previous definition of total order ( OrdLogic ) relied on the comparison function cmp_log (the logic counterpart to cmp ), which returns an Ordering . // Old definition of total order pub trait OrdLogic { # [ logic ] fn cmp_log ( self , other : Self ) -> Ordering ; // ... (laws and other comparison operators) } That had the benefit of making totality an implicit consequence of the type of the function: any two elements must compare either Less , Equal , or Greater . With the switch to partial orders, a traditional formulation based on a boolean comparison function (" < ", aka. lt_log ) becomes more natural. A strict partial order ( PartialOrdLogic ) consists of a comparison function lt_log which is irreflexive and transitive. Totality becomes another law: for all x , y , the trijunction x < y || x == y || y < x must hold. // (New) definition of partial order pub trait PartialOrdLogic { /// `self < other` in logic # [ logic ] fn lt_log ( self , other : Self ) -> bool ; // ... (laws (irreflexivity, transitivity) and other comparison operators) } // New definition of total order pub trait OrdLogic { /// The order is total # [ logic ( law )] # [ ensures ( self < other || self == other || other < self )] fn lt_log_total ( self , other : Self ); } Interestingly, none of our existing proofs were affected by this change. Our automated provers just took it in stride. Logic VC gen Creusot now generates verification conditions (VCs) for snapshots, which are logic expressions embedded in Rust programs. In particular, this enhances the use of "lemma functions", a common idiom in verification tools similar to Creusot. For example, you can encode a lemma as a logic function such as this, which logically amounts to the proposition forall<x> hyp(x) -> concl(x) : # [ logic ] # [ requires ( hyp ( x ))] # [ ensures ( concl ( x ))] fn lemma ( x : usize ) {} Then, inside a program function you can call lemma inside a snapshot! : fn f ( n : usize ) { snapshot! ( lemma ( n )); } Creusot now translates this call to an assertion that hyp(n) (the precondition of lemma ) is true and an assumption that concl(n) (its postcondition) is true. Notably, these statements are specialized to n , the argument of lemma , so we avoid relying on provers to instantiate the universal quantifier in forall<x> hyp(x) -> concl(x) . It should be said that this new feature specifically enables logic functions to be used as lemma functions. Before, you could already do something similar with program functions: # [ requires ( hyp ( x ))] #

articles.summary: EVE Online工程师分享如何利用基于头部的动态EMA和确定性采样技术，在20年历史的MMO架构中实现分布式追踪与可观测性。

articles.title: Cloudflare’s OHTTP Gateway Refuses to Decrypt Requests That Arrive through Cloudflare
articles.content: Cloudflare has opened a closed beta of its OHTTP Gateway, a managed endpoint that decrypts Oblivious HTTP requests for an origin. The design choice drawing attention is a refusal: the Gateway will not decrypt requests arriving from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare, because that would put client identifiers and request contents in the same hands. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: Cloudflare 开放 OHTTP 网关封闭测试，可解密来源服务器的匿名 HTTP 请求，但拒绝解密来自 Workers 或经 Cloudflare 代理的请求。

articles.title: Spotify More Than Doubled Monthly Code Changes as AI Accelerated Development
articles.content: Spotify reports that AI-assisted development more than doubled monthly merged changes, prompting a review of quality and reliability controls across its engineering organization. The company describes changes to testing, observability, rollback capacity, workload prioritization, and automated maintenance as it adapts to higher software change volume. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Spotify 称 AI 辅助开发使每月合并代码变更量翻倍以上，公司因此重新审查测试、可观测性和回滚等质量与可靠性控制。

articles.title: Article: When Should You Use Liquid Clustering? Benchmarking Lakehouse Layout Strategies
articles.content: Physical data layout is one of the most consequential decisions in lakehouse engineering. The author compares Liquid Clustering, ZOrdering, and partitioning across four workload types on Delta Lake, uncovering two undocumented failure modes that likely affect production systems today and offering a decision framework for choosing the right layout strategy. By Kushal Kumar Vishwakarma
articles.summary: InfoQ 文章在 Delta Lake 上对比 Liquid Clustering、ZOrdering 与分区策略，发现两种未公开的失效模式，可能影响生产系统。

articles.title: Podcast: What Does It Really Mean To Program With AI: A Conversation with Joy Ebertz
articles.content: In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Joy Ebertz about how the use of artificial intelligence is changing the way architects and developers do their jobs. Focusing on the long term success of the business is one of the most neglected tasks of an architect. This task becomes particularly important as the nature of artificial intelligence changes the landscape of software development. By Joy Ebertz
articles.summary: InfoQ 播客中 Joy Ebertz 与主持人探讨 AI 如何改变架构师和开发者的工作方式，强调关注业务长期成功的重要性。

articles.title: Presentation: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
articles.content: Erik Peterson discusses why AI spend is eclipsing cloud bills, triggering a major software engineering cost crisis. He explains tokenmaxxing, unit economics, forced developer promotions, and why fully autonomous AI will write, deploy, and govern code by 2028. By Erik Peterson
articles.summary: Erik Peterson 演讲指出 AI 支出正超过云账单，引发软件工程成本危机，并预测 2028 年全自主 AI 将编写、部署和治理代码。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第537期：Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，另有一项大型研究。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第536期：顶尖 AI 模型未能通过自主开展 AI 研究的测试，本期还关注 AI 治理、战争规划和个人电脑应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第535期：AI 成本过高，企业转向更便宜的模型，本期还关注大规模部署进入日常使用及 AI 被限制或移除的案例。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第534期：校园 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第533期：Meta 被曝其 AI 电话代理背后有真人呼叫者，揭示自动化呼叫、隐私提示和监控中的隐藏人工介入。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第531期：AI 实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前就发布代理，本期关注隐私泄露、模型自写记忆和监管问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第530期：企业为 AI 分配具体任务，如检查监控、帮助农民理解记录、搜索卫星图像和准备销售报价。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第529期：OpenAI 因 ChatGPT 涉嫌伤害面临 50 多起诉讼，其中 30 起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第528期：盘点企业实际用 AI 构建的项目，包括诊断样本无人机、无人驾驶卡车、维修副驾等 136 个用例。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #527: Schools are choosing opposite futures for AI
articles.content: One University of Chicago curriculum is removing AI-assisted writing from the classroom. Alpha School is expanding a model that puts adaptive software at the center of the academic day. The strongest signal in the latest Who’s Who Global Edition is that education is moving past general principles and into incompatible operating designs.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第527期：学校对 AI 选择截然相反的未来，芝加哥大学课程移除 AI 辅助写作，Alpha School 则扩大自适应软件教学。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述一个 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为容器隔离的企业 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将于 9 月 17 日在 PlanetScale 旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI、开发工具和人们正在构建的东西展开交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 在播客中提出开源仓库可能已被大规模攻陷的猜想，并讨论 AI 如何改变知识图谱与开发格局。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 推出 5 美元 Postgres 服务，Sam Lambert 介绍 Vitess 重写、AI 代理部署数据库变更及 500TB 表秒级回滚等能力。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 与 Canarytokens 蜜罐工具，分享攻击者最常触发的 AWS API 密钥陷阱等实战经验。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 讲述从 react-boilerplate、styled-components 等开源项目到加入 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与平台建设的历程。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 讲解服务端 Code Mode 如何让单个 MCP 服务器用约 1000 token 暴露全部约 2500 个 API 端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative 创始人 Adam Jacob 分享 AI 代理重塑软件开发后，团队从 18 人缩减至 5 人、四周内发布 Swamp 900 次的经验。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI 遭 Checkmarx 供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta 编译器改用 Go 重写提速约 10 倍，pgBackRest 维护者离职。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师 Amelia Wattenberger 探讨 AI 代理时代软件开发最后 30% 的工作为何可能成为最难的部分，并分享在 Augment Code 的设计实践。

articles.title: GTA 6 Is Reportedly Coming to PC In Early 2027
articles.content: GamesBeat reports that Rockstar plans to release Grand Theft Auto VI on PC in the first quarter of 2027, just a few months after its November 19, 2026 launch on consoles. The report follows Microsoft's announcement last week that it had secured exclusive cloud-streaming rights to the game. Since Rockstar has yet to officially announce a PC version, "this deal will allow Xbox to market its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to PC players who would otherwise need an Xbox Series X / S or PS5 console," The Verge reported at the time. GamesBeat reports: The Q1 2027 PC release window for GTA VI comes only a few months after the game's November 2026 console launch, representing a significantly quicker turnaround for PC development than the previous iteration of Grand Theft Auto, whose April 2015 PC release came roughly a year and seven months after the September 2013 release of Grand Theft Auto V. The user base of Grand Theft Auto V skews largely towards console players, with PC players representing a small minority. With GTA VI's production budget rumored to exceed $2 billion, Rockstar is highly incentivized to pull all the levers it can as fast as it can to monetize the game's upcoming sequel -- and PC players represent a significant expansion of the GTA VI audience. The potential benefits of launching GTA VI relatively quickly on PC go beyond the opportunity to grow the game's casual player base. Rockstar has signaled its plans to implement user-generated content creation tools into GTA VI, and the company's August 2023 acquisition of Cfx.re, the development team behind the prominent Grand Theft Auto V roleplaying server company FiveM, made it clear that Rockstar considers online roleplaying in GTA to be a factor in the game's future. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 据 GamesBeat 报道，Rockstar 计划于 2027 年第一季度将《GTA 6》带到 PC 平台，此前主机版定于 2026 年 11 月发售。

articles.title: Disney Offers $20 Million For Character.AI Assets As Startup Files For Bankruptcy
articles.content: Character.AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and plans to sell substantially all of its assets, with Disney offering $20 million as a "stalking-horse bidder" for select intellectual property and company claims. However, the company said Disney's bid is subject to "higher or better offers." Deadline reports: The company, which allows users to create and interact with AI-generated avatars, said it made the filing in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. It said it hopes the process will allow it to "facilitate a value-maximizing sale of all or substantially all" of its assets. The Character.AI platform will continue to operate during the bankruptcy. The Disney agreement, reached prior to the filing, would give the media giant a non-exclusive perpetual license of select intellectual property and company claims from Character.AI. Disney would pay $20 million and provide resources during a transition period as the company explores a sale. [...] Character.AI said it is aiming to conclude the sale process by late November or early December. Character.AI has faced a series of controversies over the past year or so. Most notably, the company settled multiple lawsuits alleging its chatbots encouraged self-harm and suicide among teenagers, including a high-profile case involving 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III. The company also faces lawsuits from Kentucky, which alleges its chatbots encouraged self-harm, and Pennsylvania, which claims the bots illegally impersonated licensed doctors. The latter allegations follow earlier complaints that Character.AI's therapy chatbots engaged in the unlicensed practice of medicine. In September 2025, Disney accused Character.AI of copyright infringement and using its characters in chatbots that were "sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children," prompting their removal from the platform. These mounting legal challenges and regulatory scrutiny ultimately contributed to this eventual bankruptcy
articles.summary: Character.AI 申请破产保护并出售资产，迪士尼以 2000 万美元作为首轮竞标者收购部分知识产权，交易仍可能被更高报价取代。

articles.title: Kroger to Lay Off 3,000 Corporate Employees In AI Restructuring
articles.content: Kroger says it will cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years as it expands its use of AI and other technology to streamline operations. "Technology is reshaping what's possible," CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. "The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done." ABC News reports: Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant "to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes." Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith's and Fred Meyer. Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO. Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart's U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart's digital capabilities. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Kroger 宣布未来三年裁减 3000 个企业岗位，借助 AI 等技术精简运营，CEO 称技术正在重塑工作方式。

articles.title: Anthropic Bans Cruelty Toward Claude
articles.content: New submitter CubicleZombie writes: Anthropic has updated its Usage Policy to prohibit "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its Claude AI models. While ordinary frustration, criticism, and adversarial testing remain acceptable, repeated cruelty could result in account restrictions. Anthropic acknowledges there's no evidence Claude can suffer but argues that uncertainty about AI consciousness warrants precaution. Critics contend the policy anthropomorphizes software, encourages unhealthy emotional attachments, and raises questions about how customers may interact with products they've paid for. The move raises an intriguing question: If an AI cannot demonstrably experience suffering, is abusing it an ethical problem, or is Anthropic simply policing human behavior? Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Anthropic 更新使用政策，禁止对 Claude 模型进行持续且不必要的虐待或残忍行为，普通批评与对抗测试仍被允许。

articles.title: Google Launches Flagship AI Model Gemini 4 Argon
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: Alphabet's Google on Wednesday released its flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon to developers and businesses worldwide, seeking to regain ground against rivals OpenAI and Anthropic after months of delays and a leadership shakeup at its DeepMind lab. The model excels at "deep work" on complex, multi-step tasks in coding, finance, law, cybersecurity and science, Google said. API pricing at launch starts at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with rates set to double after November 30. [...] Argon is available to paying customers through the company's AI application building tools. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can access it through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, while the Antigravity coding tool is limited to Ultra subscribers. Teams using Argon in Antigravity increased agentic code submissions by more than 35%, while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third, Google said. Google also announced the expansion of its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners. "The program gives vetted cybersecurity defenders a version of Argon without its cyber guardrails," reports Reuters. "In September, the company had said it was providing the model to select cybersecurity partners." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 谷歌发布旗舰 AI 模型 Gemini 4 Argon，面向全球开发者与企业开放，力图在延迟和 DeepMind 人事变动后追赶 OpenAI 与 Anthropic。

articles.title: FBI Arrests Canadian Cybersecurity Expert In ShinyHunters Hacking Case
articles.content: Canadian cybersecurity figures say they were shocked after ransomware negotiator Edward Dubrovsky was reportedly arrested in Pennsylvania in connection with the FBI's ShinyHunters hacking investigation. "We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," wrote FBI Director Kash Patel on social media. CBC News reports: Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers. Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats. The allegations have not been proven in court. "For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday. Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened." "This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well." ShinyHunters is one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups that's been tied to major campaigns, including a recent breach involving FBI employee data, a cyberattack on Canvas, as well as various cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, and Ticketmaster. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 加拿大网络安全专家 Edward Dubrovsky 因 FBI 的 ShinyHunters 黑客调查在宾州被捕，业界对此表示震惊。

articles.title: Microsoft Reveals Maia 300 AI Chip As It Works To Reduce Dependence On Nvidia
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Yahoo Finance: Microsoft has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia and AMD. Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year. The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services." The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200. [...] The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. articles.title: Mutative v2  - better immutability and faster immutable updates
articles.content: Mutative 2.0 is out. Read the release notes , the announcement and the migration guide from v1 to v2 . Mutative - A JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates ( documentation ). In the benchmark , it was about 3.6x faster than Immer with the same settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults across 97 workloads. In that benchmark the gap widened on large arrays, where Mutative moved elements up to 1,052x faster than Immer. When copying dominates, such as updating objects with thousands of keys, inserting at the front of a large array or adding an item to a large Set, Mutative is even faster than hand-written reducers. How does Mutative compare with the spread operation (hand-written reducers)? Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes. Immer made it easy to write immutable updates as mutations of a draft. Mutative keeps that model and focuses on performance: it copies each object at most once per update, drafts objects only when a recipe reads them, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and runs array methods that move elements natively on its copies. Immer freezes the next state by default, which costs time on every update; Mutative freezes it only when asked to. Mutative also takes its options per call instead of from global configuration, drafts class instances through marks instead of changing their classes, supports async recipes and Map and Set subclasses, and handles edge cases that Immer gets wrong. Comparison with Immer lists the differences. Mutative passed all of Immer's test cases. Mutative 2.0.0 was 3.6x faster than Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, on geometric mean across 97 benchmarked workloads, and faster in 595 of 614 measured cases. The gap grows on large arrays, where Mutative moves elements natively: removing the first of 10,000 rows took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs. With matched settings, both libraries freeze or both do not, and both generate patches or both do not. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases. The other 3 return a state that Immer froze earlier: Immer skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searches it unless the recipe wraps it in rawReturn() , which took 0.26 µs. articles.title: Type-safe OpenAPI requests that follow your document exactly
articles.content: openapi-chain compiles the serialization rules an OpenAPI document declares (parameter style , explode , allowReserved and content , request media types, and form and multipart Encoding Objects) and applies them to every request. A build-time CLI generates types and metadata scoped to the paths you call, so large documents stay affordable to type-check and to ship. Calls use a fluent path API with no generated endpoint code and no runtime dependencies. The pnpm monorepo contains three publishable packages: openapi-chain , @openapi-chain/cli , and @openapi-chain/query . The runtime keeps its existing package name and entry points. See the package migration guide for CLI and query import changes and release availability. The first request below uses the Items schema . Your chain follows your own schema: static path segments become properties, {parameters} become function calls, and HTTP methods become request functions. Exact wire serialization: the strict client sends what the document specifies and rejects representations it cannot encode instead of guessing. The wire comparison executes 20 declarations through both clients: openapi-fetch 0.17.0 sends a request with different values, media type or missing parameters in 16 of them, and differs only in percent-encoding or list spacing in 3 more. Scoped generation for large documents: one CLI config produces full declarations, a path scope and matching runtime metadata. On the pinned GitHub REST document, scoping a 40-operation consumer reduced openapi-chain's TypeScript 7 check time from 0.49 s to 0.045 s ( real-schema measurements ). Typed requests and responses: infer parameters, request media types and status-correlated results from the selected operation. Keep openapi-fetch if you already use it: openapi-chain/openapi-fetch applies the same serialization to an existing openapi-fetch client ( adapter guide ). Small schema-free core: the default client has a 3.5 KiB gzip budget , enforced by a reproducible size check ; its bundle size and per-request overhead are in the same range as openapi-fetch ( client comparison ). Customizable requests: operation-typed extensions and Fetch-compatible transports support application-specific serialization, authentication and parsing. When to choose openapi-chain Choose the strict client when your document declares non-default parameter styles, parameter content , cookie parameters, non-JSON media types or form and multipart encoding, and the server depends on them. Choose the CLI's scoped generation when a large document makes type-checking or metadata delivery expensive. If your API only uses JSON bodies and default parameter styles, openapi-fetch and openapi-chain's core are comparable in size and speed; pick the call style you prefer. Without scoping, openapi-chain's fluent types cost more to check than openapi-fetch's on the measured GitHub and Stripe documents. For a published release with this API: pnpm add openapi-chain pnpm add -D @openapi-chain/cli S

Instead, Vite+ ties the tools you already use into one tested stack with a single config file and a consistent set of commands. Vite+ is free, open source under MIT , and framework-agnostic. Whether you ship a React app, a Vue component library, a Node CLI, or a 400-package monorepo, the commands stay the same. Your project does not even have to use Vite in the first place! Starting a web project means a lot of choices to make before even starting to write your first line of code: picking a runtime, choosing a package manager, deciding on a dev server, setting up a linter, a formatter, a test runner, a bundler, you name it. Each one brings its own config files, release cadence, commands, and its own upgrade guide. And that matters for you at least twice . First when you pick the tool stack (or get onboarded to it), then every time things drift apart: the linter disagrees with the formatter, CI runs different commands than you do locally, one repo is two majors behind another, and the person who originally set it up is on vacation. Teams with more than a handful of repositories usually end up building internal scripts to paper over this, which then need their own maintainers. Node.js now ships a built-in for each of them. Here are twelve of those built-ins, with the package each one replaces, the shortest example that runs, how stable it is in the current LTS line, and the one thing the old package still does that the built-in doesn’t. Several of these changed status in the last year, so I checked every claim against the Node 24 API docs (24.21.0, the Active LTS line as of September 2026) and ran every example on Node 26.0.0, which is what node --version prints on my Mac. Node 22 is in maintenance until April 2027, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026, and Node 26 becomes the next LTS on October 28, 2026. Where Node 22 and 24 differ, I say so. A quick reminder on how Node labels its APIs. Stability 2 is stable. Stability 1 is experimental, with sub-levels: 1.0 is early development, 1.1 is active development, 1.2 is a release candidate. Anything experimental can change or disappear in a minor release, so the number matters if you’re putting it in production. 1. node:sqlite replaces better-sqlite3 For years the way to use SQLite from Node was better-sqlite3 , a native addon you had to compile (or download a prebuilt binary for) on every install. Node 22.5 added a SQLite driver to core. Like better-sqlite3 , it’s synchronous, so the code reads top to bottom with no await . import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite' const db = new DatabaseSync ( '/Users/flavio/notes.db' ) db. exec ( 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)' ) const insert = db. prepare ( 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)' ) insert. run ( 'Buy espresso beans' ) console. log (db. prepare ( 'SELECT * FROM notes' ). all ()) The module only exists under the node: prefix, a plain import 'sqlite' fails. Status in Node 24: 1.2, release candidate , since 24.15.0. It prints no warning. You write those three statements yourself in a try / catch . I show the pattern in node:sqlite: SQLite built into Node.js , and the free SQLite course covers transactions and indexes in more depth. 2. node:test and node:assert replace Jest and Mocha Jest was the default test runner for a long time, and I have a whole post on it from 2018. articles.title: Tibetan-Singing-Bowls: Strike or rub a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls - synthesized in the browser with Web Audio, with the beating overtones of the real thing
articles.content: Play a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls right in your browser. Strike a bowl, or hold it down to draw the tone out the way a mallet circles the rim. The sound is synthesized live, so there are no audio files to load, and it works offline. Use headphones or good speakers. Seven bowls are tuned to a scale, each with its own color. Tap or click a bowl to strike it. Switch to Sing and hold a bowl down to make it swell and sustain, then let go to let it fade. The number keys 1 to 7 play the bowls from the keyboard, and you can play several at once. Tuning : a seven-note chakra scale (C to B, one bowl per chakra) or a pentatonic scale, in the low, middle or high octave, with A at 440 Hz or 432 Hz. Sound : volume and room reverb. Spectrum : a live view of the sound, so you can watch the overtones rise and fade. Sound bath : press start and pick 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes, and the bowls play by themselves, one strike at a time, with silence in between. A struck bowl rings at its fundamental plus overtones at about 2.7, 5.2 and 8.3 times that pitch. Those overtones are not whole-number multiples, which is why a bowl sounds like a bell and not like a string. Each partial is made of two sine oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, so it swells and fades a few times a second: that beating is the "wah-wah" of a real bowl. Higher partials die away faster. The result goes through a synthesized room reverb and a compressor. This is a model of the sound and not a recording. The bowls are not meant as a medical treatment, and the chakra colors are a common convention, not a measurement. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API, with no dependencies and no build step. Just open index.html . It is also a small installable web app: add it to your home screen or desktop and it works offline. The bowls are drawn as SVG. The app logic is in js/bowls.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. Your tuning, volume and other settings are kept in the browser's local storage. articles.title: Supapower - A sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase, inspired by PowerSync
articles.content: Supapower is a sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase , so an application can read and write locally and stay usable while offline. It is inspired by PowerSync . Status: 0.3.0. Both directions of the sync work; the public API may still change before 1.0. Nothing new to deploy - Supabase's Data API and Realtime are the sync protocol; no sync service, no replication slot, no second bill. Real Postgres on both ends - the client is PGlite, not SQLite: the same SQL, the same types, and migrations you can lift from the server. Your RLS policies are the sync rules - downloads and writes go through PostgREST as the signed-in user, so there is no second authorization language to keep in step. Two-way sync that merges per column - offline writes queue per transaction and upload only the columns that changed, so two people editing different fields of a row both keep their edit. Three lines to adopt - a PGlite extension plus one sync() call; no codegen, no schema DSL, no client-side query language to learn. Small, permissive, batteries included - Apache-2.0 with zero runtime dependencies, plus a SharedWorker multi-tab host, React and Vue bindings, and a typed status and event API. articles.title: 关于长辈抽烟的问题，有好的解决办法么？
articles.content:
家里住的是 2 梯 4 户的住宅，中间有一条比较长的公共连廊。

我爸前几年又开始抽烟了，其实他之前已经戒了很多年。后来因为抽烟比较多，经常咳嗽，还戒过一段时间，但这几年又抽上了。

我和我妈都劝不动他，慢慢也就默认了，只要他不在家里抽就行。平时他有时候在连廊抽，有时候在楼梯口抽。

最近因为这件事，邻居找上门了。

邻居之前当面跟我爸沟通过，但我爸不太搭理她。后来她也找我说过几次，我其实挺理解她的，毕竟大家住得近，出门或者刚好经过的时候，迎面碰到烟味，确实会让人不舒服。

但问题是，我之前也跟我爸沟通过好几次了，每次说到抽烟的事情，他脾气都比较大，最后基本都会吵一架，实际效果也不怎么样。

说实话，我自己也不喜欢烟味，每次闻到我爸身上的烟味，我也挺难受的。我当然也希望他能改掉这个习惯，但他毕竟是成年人，我和我妈确实很难管得住他。

今天邻居又来找我沟通这件事，我一下子又开始内耗了。

一方面，我能理解邻居的感受，也觉得她提出的问题确实有道理；另一方面，我也不知道还能怎么处理。继续找我爸沟通，大概率又是一顿争吵，而且未必有效果。不管吧，又觉得对邻居有些过意不去。

现在感觉自己夹在中间，两边都不好处理。

想问问站里的朋友，如果遇到这种情况，有没有什么比较好的处理办法？

我的主要诉求其实很简单，就是想尽量把这个问题解决掉，不要让邻居继续受到影响，也不想因为这件事跟我爸反复吵架，更不希望最后闹成邻里矛盾。

有没有什么相对可行的办法，能让这件事得到改善？
articles.summary: 网友求助：父亲在公共连廊抽烟引发邻居投诉，多次沟通均以争吵收场，寻求有效解决办法。

##  背景

公司前阵子收到了律师函，于是通知全员删除 navicat ，个人版也不行，要求用开源的 DBeaver ，由于常年习惯了 navicat 的布局和操作习惯，实在适应不了其他工具，都 AI 时代了，索性自己撸一个吧。


## 技术栈 & 进度

Rust + GPUI ，gpui-kit 组件库 , shadcn 风格。无 WebView ，全部 UI 都用 Rust 写

适配了 ODBC 驱动，理论上只要有 ODBC 驱动，都能连接

| -------------------------- | ---------------- |
| MySQL / MariaDB            | ✅        |
| SQLite                     | ✅        |
| SQL Server                 | ✅        |
| PostgreSQL                 | ✅        |
| Oracle                     | ✅        |
| DB2, Redis, ...           | 接入中 |

articles.title: 2026 年了，还有老架构坚持 MySQL 单表数据不能超过 2000 万行
articles.content:
问他为什么，张口闭口就是：“单表过 2000 万，B+ 树就从 3 层变成 4 层了，多一层就多一次磁盘 I/O ，多的我不想说了 你自己问 AI”

我寻思现在生产环境服务器 256G 内存，给 Buffer Pool 分 200G 。

Buffer Pool 看着 200G 空间表示：“我管你这那的，非叶子节点全都给我常驻内存！多出来的一层不过是几十纳秒的内存二分查找，哪来的这么多废话”

业务场景如果是因为备份恢复 SLA 扛不住、在线 DDL 风险大、或者热数据 Working Set 超出内存导致离散回表击穿，那该分分、该归档归档，这叫架构治理；
但如果不看硬件规格和查询场景，纯拿“B+ 树长到 4 层就会性能崩塌”当圣经到处念咒，AI 的回复直接输出本帖
